sense: ought to: what is right or expected

terms.grammar: verb, impersonal, with an infinitive, an accusative and infinitive, or a bare subjunctive
evidence: Cato Agr. 3.1: aedificāre diū cōgitāre oportet
terms.comment: What is fitting or to be expected. “Should have” is oportuit with the infinitive: cēnam jam esse coctam oportuit, dinner should have been cooked by now; mōrem gestum oportuit, you should have humoured him.

terms.grammar: verb, second conjugation, with an infinitive
evidence: Sen. Ep. 28.1: animum dēbēs mūtāre, nōn caelum
Cic. Sen. 69: eō dēbet esse contentus
terms.comment: A duty owed: “you ought to”. Not for what is merely likely, nor for what has to be (see must).

evidence: Traupman 97, 305: it won’t do to (+ inf.), nōn satis est
terms.comment: Nōn satis est is “it is not enough” (nōn satis est ars sōla cocō, Mart. 14.220.1; see too little). For “it won’t do to …” say nōn oportet (above).

phrases.latin: aedificāre diū cōgitāre oportet, cōnserere cōgitāre nōn oportet, sed facere oportet
phrases.english: you should think long about building; about planting you shouldn’t think, you should just do it

phrases.latin: properāte, cēnam jam esse coctam oportuit.
phrases.english: Hurry up: dinner should have been cooked by now.

phrases.latin: Tua culpa. — Quid agerem? — Adulēscentī mōrem gestum oportuit.
phrases.english: Your fault. — What was I to do? — You should have humoured the young man.

phrases.latin: parce gaudēre oportet et sēnsim querī
phrases.english: one should rejoice sparingly and complain slowly
you ought to change your mind, not your sky
we ought, as they say, to copy the bees

debeo.html: With an infinitive dēbeō speaks of a duty; for what simply has to be, Latin says necesse est. Lewis & Short: in classical prose always of moral necessity.

sources: Lewis & Short: oportet · Lewis & Short: debeo
